newsitem.title: POLAND: Zloty key to 1997 Polish monetary policy - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Zloty key to 1997 Polish monetary policy - central bank.

text.p: The key challenge for Poland's central bank next year will be to keep the zloty exchange rate at levels which will cap the current account deficit and help reduce inflation, the bank's deputy president said.

"In my opinion the key dilemma of monetary policy next year will not be interest rates but what...could be the acceptable rate of the crawling devaluation from the point of view of our inflation goals," Witold Kozinski told Reuters in an interview.
The government aims to reduce year-on-year inflation in December 1997 to 13 percent from an expected 17.9-18.2 percent at the end of this year.

Kozinski said the bank saw little upside potential for the zloty next year, expecting rather market pressure for a deeper depreciation than the planned nine-percent crawling devaluation of the zloty's central parity rate.
"There will likely be a situation that a (relative) scarcity of currencies will translate into pressure on zloty devaluation against the basket of currencies," Kozinski said.
The zloty is now devalued by one percent a month, 12.7 percent a year, against a basket of western currencies.
In its monetary policy guidelines for next year the NBP said it wanted to cut the devaluation factor so that the Polish unit would weaken by nine percent in 1997.

The forecasts are based on expectations that imports would continue to rise faster next year resulting in a widening of the current account gap to about $3.9 billion from this year's expected $300 million and reserves flat at this year's levels.
Kozinski said a fall in reserves would have a deflationary effect but the central bank would not accept a deep decline in net foreign reserves, seen rising this year by $2.3 billion to $22.7 billion.
"The NBP is unlikely to just look on if reserves will be falling," he said adding the bank might allow the market to correct the situation by weakening the zloty.

But he said the bank would keep markets guessing over how much movement it would allow within the 14-percent trading band on the domestic forex market and the uncertainty, combined with devaluation expectations, would cap short-term capital flows.

"I believe there will be no problem with short-term capital in 1997, also because of our (unpredictable) behaviour -- we can either reduce the crawl or not, we can slow-down the zloty's fall, if it happens, but we could intervene the other way as well," Kozinski said.
He said the uncertainty would give the National Bank of Poland more freedom in pursuing higher real interest rates.
"Our interest rate policy is straightforward -- inflation will be falling but rates will stay constant," Kozinski said.
The NBP has said it had to allow real rates to rise in order slow fast credit expansion and booming domestic demand. @
Kozinski said higher rates combined with a possibly weaker zloty should form a natural defensive against a deeper deterioration of Poland's current account and depletion of its reserves.
Kozinski said the bank would not prevent market interest rates from rising in the near future because the money supply growth target for this year has been already overshot.
But he said in the longer term the bank might have to offer help to the system if it is squeezed by falling foreign exchange reserves and turns underliquid.
"It can be a perspective of next year but it is still only a possibility and my feeling is that if direct investment kicks in more strongly the shortage of funds may not materialise," Kozinski said.

But if there was a real threat of the market turning illiquid the NBP would rather focus on limiting the scope of its draining operations and later cut mandatory reserves than rely on repo operations, he added.
